title: What If You Got Hotter and Couldn't Stop?
premise: A thought experiment, not a forecast: your temperature climbs from 37 °C to the edge of physics in under a minute while you stand in a snowy field at night and watch your own heat light, burn and then bleach out everything around you; the temperatures are real and the body that survives them is pretend.
audience: YouTube Shorts viewers who watch 'what if' science scenarios told in the second person with counters, on a phone, often muted.
question: If you kept getting hotter, how far could it go, and is there a point where it has to stop?
share_line: you are literally glowing right now and nobody can see it
comment_prompt: The film asks nothing on screen. The caption asks one easy question (what viewers thought the hottest thing was) and the first comment another (the highest their own thermometer has read). What viewers will have something to say about in the film itself: the rule 'The metal tungsten boils here. Pretend you don't.' and the clock row that reads PRETEND BODY (jokes about the person still standing there); 'Red is the coolest glow there is' (people who assumed red-hot was the top); whether 10^32 K is really a limit (the film says nobody knows); and the last three words, plus the NEXT row that ends on STAY HERE.
post_caption: You start at 37 °C. Forty-five seconds later, physics runs out of answers. What did you think was the hottest thing there is? Every temperature on the counter is real; the body that survives them is not.
first_comment: The one made-up thing here is you. A real body is in danger at the first step: heat stroke, at 41 °C (106 °F), can kill without emergency treatment. People often say lightning is hotter than the Sun. Hotter than its surface, about five times over (0:35); the Sun's core is about 500 times hotter than lightning. And the snowflake melts because your skin is warm, not because it can see infrared. Sources are in the description. What is the highest your own thermometer has ever read?
first_comment_note: For the creator to post and pin under the Short. It carries the disclosures that the description holds but few Shorts viewers open. Do not add a personal anecdote unless the creator supplies a true one.
post_description:
Your temperature starts at 37 °C and climbs for one minute without stopping. You stay where you are, in a snowy field at night, and watch what your own heat does to it.

WHAT IS REAL: the temperatures on the counter. Normal body temperature is taken as 37 °C. In heat stroke the body can reach 41 °C or more, and without emergency treatment that can kill. Water boils at 100 °C at sea level, and up to 60% of an adult body is water. Solids begin to give off a dull red glow at roughly 525 °C (an approximate figure). Glowing lava is red at about 600 to 800 °C, orange up to 1,000 °C and yellow up to 1,200 °C: red is the coolest glow there is. Iron melts at 1,538 °C. Tungsten boils at 5,555 °C. The Sun's visible surface is about 5,500 °C. Lightning heats the air to about 28,000 °C. Above roughly 10,000 degrees a glowing object gives off mostly ultraviolet, and above a million mostly X-rays, so to the eye the colour stops at blue-white. The Sun's core is about 15 million °C; that figure comes from models of the Sun, not from a measurement. About 4 trillion °C has been made and measured at Brookhaven's RHIC collider, hot enough that protons and neutrons melt into a soup of quarks and gluons. The Planck temperature is about 1.4 x 10^32 kelvin. And at 37 °C you really do glow, in infrared.

WHAT IS MADE UP, OR NOT KNOWN: you. A real body stops being alive near the second step and would be gas long before the Sun's surface. The film pretends yours holds together and keeps being fed energy; that is the one impossible thing in it. Everything the field does (the red light on the snow, the fence burning, the ground glowing, how far your light reaches) is an illustration built on rough sums that treat you as a perfect radiator of 1.8 square metres with no air in the way. Real air would turn into a fireball. Past the Sun's surface the honest view is only too bright to look at, so the rings, the grain at 4 trillion degrees and the still white at the end are drawings. How fast the counter climbs was chosen to fit a minute. The Planck temperature is not a proven limit: it is where today's physics stops being able to say what happens, and physicists do not agree on whether a highest temperature exists. The snowflake melts because your skin is warm, not because it can see infrared.

SOURCES: MedlinePlus (body temperature) https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001982.htm | NASA Science (infrared) https://science.nasa.gov/ems/07_infraredwaves/ | CDC NIOSH (heat stroke) https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/heat-stress/about/illnesses.html | USGS (water) https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/water-science-school/science/facts-about-water and https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/water-science-school/science/water-you-water-and-human-body | Draper point https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draper_point | USGS (lava) https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/how-hot-a-hawaiian-volcano | WebElements (iron, tungsten) https://www.webelements.com/iron/ and https://www.webelements.com/tungsten/ | NASA (the Sun) https://science.nasa.gov/sun/facts/ and https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html | US National Weather Service (lightning) https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-temperature | OpenStax Astronomy 2e, 5.2 (colour and temperature) https://openstax.org/books/astronomy-2e/pages/5-2-the-electromagnetic-spectrum | Brookhaven (4 trillion degrees) https://www.bnl.gov/newsroom/news.php?a=23161 | CERN (quark-gluon plasma) https://home.cern/science/physics/heavy-ions-and-quark-gluon-plasma | NIST (Planck temperature) https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?plktmp | PBS NOVA, Absolute Hot https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/zero/hot.html

lines.text: Twenty-five seconds ago, you stood in snow.

beats.picture: The film's own 28.0-31.0 s, shown first. You stand on bare scorched ground that glows dull orange in a patch round your feet. Hard yellow-white light pours outward from where you stand, as if you were the lamp. A line of fence posts runs away from you; the near ones are burning stumps, and every post throws a long black shadow pointing straight away from you. A far ridge is lit like noon under a black sky with no stars. No snow anywhere. Light: yellow-white, and it is yours.
beats.motion: Picture, both counters and the line are complete on frame 0: no fade up. The temperature climbs about 50 °C a second and the clock runs in tenths, so the two numbers disagree from the first frame. Shadows quiver, sparks lift off the stumps, the lit circle on the ground widens by a post or two, the camera turns slowly right along the fence. At 3.0 s the figures spin back in a few frames and the scene flips to night in one frame; no black frame, and the counters never leave.

lines.text: What If You Got Hotter and Couldn't Stop?
A snowflake melts on your palm.

beats.picture: The same spot, twenty-five seconds earlier: a flat snow-covered field at night under stars, snow falling slowly. The fence posts stand whole, each with a cap of snow: the first 1.6 m to your left, the second at 5 m, then one every 5 m to a low ridge about 2.2 km off. Your own bare palm comes up into the bottom of the frame; one snowflake lands on it and melts to a bead of water. Light: deep blue starlight. Nothing glows.
beats.motion: The title sits in the clear sky above the ridge, centred, not across the posts, and is up for 2.6 s. The palm rises at 3.6 s as the camera tilts down a little; the flake lands at 4.9 s and is a bead by 5.7 s, before the line names it at 5.9 s. The temperature figure has started to move: 37.1 as the palm rises, 37.2 as the flake lands, 37.3 by 6.5 s. During the line two more flakes land, each melting sooner than the last, and the next ones vanish just above the skin. The line leaves at 8.5 s. The palm lowers out of frame by 9.0 s (38.7 °C) and is not seen again until the close; the camera tilts back up along the fence.
beats.sound: Quiet bed, no pulse yet. One small bright note as the flake melts (4.9 s): the object's own sound, used again at the close.
beats.uses: patterns.md Hook 4 (reference 6.5-10.3 s): back to the ordinary start, title as a question, the only text in the middle of the frame. Structure 6 (25.0 s): plant an ordinary object early. Look 2: something of the viewer's own in frame (a palm here, newly made). Holding attention 5: the picture leads the words.

lines.text: Forty-one. Heat stroke. It can kill.
One hundred. The water in you boils.

beats.picture: The field ahead; your body is out of frame from here on. The falling snow stops reaching you: an empty bubble in the snowfall, an arm's length wide. Then the flakes at the bubble's edge flash into steam, and a ring of dark wet earth opens in the snow at the bottom of the frame. Light: still blue night; the steam is grey-blue.
beats.motion: 9.2 s: the bubble in the snowfall opens, with no line over it for its first second. The figure holds near 41 while the first line is up (41.0 at 10.2 s, 42.3 when it leaves at 12.6 s), then runs from 42.5 to 100 in half a second (13.0-13.5 s). 13.2 s: first hiss of steam, a moment before the second line. The wet ring creeps out to the first post, whose snow cap slides off at 15.0 s. The second line leaves at 16.2 s. Steam rolls up across the stars. The figure drops its decimal at 100 (a change of form). The clock row flips to PRETEND BODY at 10.2 s.

lines.text: The Sun's core. Humans have gone hotter.

beats.picture: The light turns blue-white and the glare climbs the frame from the ground up: the glowing earth, the last stumps, then the ridge, each bleaching out in turn. For a second the ridge is a thin dark line in the white; then it is gone. After that the frame is blue-white with nothing in it but slow rings of slightly brighter light travelling outward from you. Light: blue-white, and it stops changing colour.
beats.motion: 34.4-35.0 s: the figure runs from 9,500 to 28,500 and the light turns blue-white just before the line. The glare rises through 35-38.8 s; the first line leaves at 37.9 s, and the ridge's last dark line goes out at 38.8 s, as the second line arrives, so the last object in the scene leaves on that line. The figure changes form at a million (digits to words, 38.3 s) and passes 15 million at 38.8 s; it keeps climbing through the line, to 250 million by 40.6 s and about 55 billion when the line leaves at 41.5 s, which is the line's point: the counter is already far past the core. The rings quicken with the counter. Counters and lines switch to dark ink as the frame whitens.

Holding attention 10: the scene empties as the scale grows, without the stillness (Do not copy: 437-496 s). Brief ruling: past the Sun's surface the colour of the light and the counter carry it.

lines.text: Humans have made this. Protons melt.

beats.picture: The even white breaks into a fine boiling grain, like static seen from very close, faintly tinted: the drawing for protons and neutrons melting into a soup of quarks and gluons. Light: white.
beats.motion: 41.6-42.3 s: the figure runs from 100 billion to 4 trillion and the grain appears just before the line. The figure holds at 4.0-4.4 trillion while the line is up. From 45.1 s there is no line for 3.1 s, the longest silence in the film: the figure changes to powers of ten in kelvin and the exponent ticks from 13 to 32, about seven a second, while the grain gets finer and faster and the NEXT row counts the powers of ten left.

beats.sound: Bed pulse at its fastest. Nothing new enters during the silence; the pulse alone tightens towards 47.8 s.
beats.uses: patterns.md Holding attention 8 (499.9-506.9 s): one long gap, placed directly before the payoff. Look 9: the figure's change of form and unit is a beat in itself.

lines.text: Here, physics runs out of answers.

beats.picture: The grain is gone in one frame: flat, even, quiet white, the plainest picture in the film. The figure has stopped on 1.4 x 10^32 K with a question mark after it. Light: white, unchanging.
beats.motion: 47.8 s: the grain stops, the figure stops, the NEXT row turns to NOBODY KNOWS with a question mark where the countdown was, and the comparison row reads AS HOT AS PHYSICS CAN DESCRIBE. The clock keeps running in tenths, the question mark pulses once a second and the white breathes very slightly at its edges, so the frame is never frozen.

beats.uses: patterns.md Structure 8 (505.5-506.9 s): payoff picture then payoff line, at 0.80 of the run as 'At 60 seconds' asks. Look 11: the NEXT row ends on its own punchline. Structure 7 (445 s): what is not known is said on screen. Sound 4-5: the one large drop, with a tick each second.

lines.text: In infrared. Your eyes cannot see it.

beats.on_screen: SOURCES IN THE DESCRIPTION (small capitals under the clock block, from 56.6 s, as the flake lands, to the end; shown together with the story lines on purpose)
beats.picture: The white comes apart into snow. It thins from the top into night sky and stars, and what is left of it is snow: on the ground, on the caps of the fence posts, falling. The field of 3 s, whole and blue. Your bare palm comes up into the bottom of the frame and one snowflake lands on it and melts. Light: deep blue starlight. Nothing glows that an eye can see.
beats.motion: 51.0-52.2 s: as the payoff line leaves, the white separates into sky and snowfall, with no black frame and no line over it: 1.2 s for the return to be seen before it is read. In the first six tenths (51.0-51.6 s) the figure spins back down through every form it has had and lands on 37.0 °C, where it stays. The clock does not reset. At 51.6 s the clock row returns to REAL BODY, the NEXT row reads STAY HERE and the comparison row reads AS WARM AS EVERYONE YOU KNOW. The first line of the close arrives at 52.2 s, when the field is whole again. The palm rises at 55.0 s; the flake lands at 56.6 s, as the sources tag comes on. The second line leaves at 57.4 s, so the last of the melt (57.4-58.0 s) has no line over it; the flake is a bead by 58.0 s, when the last line arrives. The film ends in motion at 59.9 s as a second flake touches the palm: no hold, no end card.

beats.sound: The bed returns at 51.0 s, quiet and without the pulse. The small bright note from 4.9 s again at 56.6 s as the flake melts. Ends on the note's tail.
beats.uses: patterns.md Structure 6 and 8 (527.7 s): end on the planted object, after a release that follows the bleakest moment (Sharing 2). Sharing 1 and 4: a short final line that can be quoted alone, and a fact about the viewer's own body with no moral drawn. Do not copy: a pointer to the sources sits on the closing picture. The reference's own ending (a loop that starts again) is not used: here the counter comes back to 37 and holds.
